title: Temperaments
hookLine: three roommates sweep one kitchen three ways; Buddhaghosa says the broom shows your temperament
tomorrow: should someone else choose your practice for you?

cards: Three roommates, one kitchen, one broom. The first sweeps slowly and evenly, gets every corner, and leaves the floor looking nice.
The second grips the broom tight and attacks the floor in quick, rough strokes, dust flying. The third pushes it around loosely, and somehow the crumbs end up where they started. Here's the odd part.
A book on the path to awakening describes nearly this exact scene. Buddhaghosa says the way you sweep can show your temperament.

teach.b: The Pali word is carita, temperament, the way a person leans. Buddhaghosa names six: the greedy, the angry, the confused, the faithful, the intelligent, and the speculative. They aren't insults.
Greedy here means drawn to what's lovely, and he pairs it with the faithful, who are moved by what's good; the angry he pairs with the intelligent, the confused with the speculative.
The clues are ordinary: posture, work, eating, what you notice first. The greedy type eats slowly and savors sweet things. The angry type eats fast and likes it rough and sour.
The confused type has no fixed taste and drops crumbs.

teach.h: MATCH THE SUBJECT TO THE PERSON.
teach.b: Then comes the matching, like medicine to a fever. The angry are given the divine abodes: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity. The greedy are given the foulness meditations, to loosen the pull of beauty.
The confused and the speculative get the breath. The faithful get the recollections of the Buddha and the teaching. And then the honest part.
Buddhaghosa admits this way of reading temperament isn't fully handed down in the texts.
It's the teachers' opinion, he says, and shouldn't be treated as certain. So hold your own guess kindly. The aim isn't a label.
It's a practice suited to you.

how: In Theravada meditation teaching, a teacher may watch how a student lives and practices before suggesting a subject; the Visuddhimagga's six temperaments are one traditional guide to that choice.

games.q: your coach notices you rush every drill and snap at teammates. by Buddhaghosa's chart, what might suit you to practice?
o: loving-kindness and the other divine abodes, to cool the heat.
the foulness meditations, to loosen the pull of nice things.
nothing yet; a temper like that has to be fixed before you start.
games.why: rushing and snapping are the angry type's clues, and Buddhaghosa gives that type the divine abodes. foulness is for the greedy type.

practice: Close your eyes and replay this morning: how you got up, how you ate, how you walked out the door. No grading. Ask the way a kind teacher would: what am I drawn to, what do I push against, where do I drift?
Let one honest guess appear, and hold it as lightly as Buddhaghosa does.

wordCard.voice: Temperaments: Buddhaghosa's six ways of leaning, from greedy to speculative, each suited to different meditation subjects.

orig.note: Pali: temperament, a person's characteristic way of behaving and leaning.

carryVoice: Here's the line: suited to you, the practice fitted to the person and not the other way around. Two of forty.
